title: Newborn behaviour and very early child development
blurb: Read a newborn's cues, support bonding and responsive feeding, track early weight and growth, and know what is checked at 6 to 8 weeks.
question: On day 5, a community midwife weighs baby Sami and finds he has lost 11% of his birth weight. His mother, Maya, is breastfeeding and says he cries a lot before feeds. What should the midwife do?

teach.body: Formally, emotional attachment is the bond a baby forms with the people who care for them, built through sensitive, consistent responses to the baby's signals. In plain English: a newborn communicates through cues (rooting, sucking a fist, crying, turning away) and grows best when someone notices and responds. NICE asks midwives to discuss bonding before and after the birth and to encourage face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin contact and responding to the baby's cues (NG194 1.3.16-1.3.17).

steps.label: Crying
steps.sub: a late cue: hard to feed

teach.caption: Feed during the early cues, because a crying baby is difficult to feed. In the first weeks expect at least 8-12 feeds in 24 hours (NHS breastfeeding guidance).

teach.body: NICE defines responsive feeding as feeding in response to the baby's cues, for love, comfort and reassurance as well as nutrition. Responsive breastfeeding also means a mother may feed for her own comfort. Responsive bottle feeding means holding the baby close, pacing the feed, recognising signs the baby has had enough and not forcing them to finish, because a formula-fed baby can be overfed. Fewer people regularly feeding the baby can help bonding, and prop feeding is dangerous (NG194 1.5.19).

items.label: Most are back to birth weight

teach.caption: Measure again around 8 weeks, and at other times only if there are concerns (NG194 1.3.6). Growth is recorded in the red book, the parent-held Personal Child Health Record (NG75 1.2.5).

teach.h: Weight loss over 10% in the early days (NG75 1.1)

root.label: Lost more than 10% of birth weight

children.label: Paediatric referral
children.sub: if illness, marked loss or no response

teach.caption: If the baby has lost over 10%, or is not back to birth weight by 3 weeks, consider paediatric referral or decide when to reassess (NG75 1.1.4).

teach.h: If a breastfed baby needs a formula supplement (NG75 1.1.6-1.1.7)
items: Be aware that supplementing may help weight gain but often leads to breastfeeding stopping.
Support the mother to continue breastfeeding.
Advise expressing breast milk to build supply.
Give any available breast milk before giving infant formula.

teach.h: Faltering growth after the early days (NG75 1.2.1)
head: Birthweight centile
Concern if weight falls across
teach.caption: A centile space is the gap between two adjacent centile lines on the UK-WHO growth chart.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Sami at the day 5 visit
teach.body: Sami has lost 11%, so the midwife does not simply reassure. She makes a clinical assessment for dehydration or illness, takes a detailed feeding history and observes a full breastfeed, checking positioning, attachment, rhythmic sucking and audible swallowing. She explains that crying is a late hunger cue and helps Maya feed at the early cues. She agrees a plan to reweigh (not more than daily) and refers to the paediatric team if he is unwell or does not respond to feeding support.

teach.h: Some families need more bonding support (NG194 1.3.18-1.3.19)

rows.label: Physical and emotional recovery from the birth
A traumatic birth or birth complications
Fatigue, sleep deprivation and feeding worries
Parents who have been through the care system
Adverse childhood experiences or complex psychosocial needs

teach.note: For babies born preterm, development is judged from the due date (corrected age) until 2 years old (NHS).

teach.text: Two traps. Crying is a LATE hunger cue, not the first one: waiting for crying makes feeding harder. And social smiling with visual fixing and following is assessed at 6 to 8 weeks (NG194 1.3.5), not in the first days, so its absence at the newborn check is expected, but its absence at 6 to 8 weeks needs further assessment.

items: Bonding: face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin and responding to cues (NG194 1.3.17).
Early hunger cues: stirring, fist sucking, murmuring, rooting; crying is late.
Weight loss usually stops by day 3-4; most babies regain birth weight by 3 weeks.
Over 10% loss: clinical assessment, feeding history, observe a feed, reweigh no more than daily.
At 6-8 weeks: social smile, fixing and following, weight and head circumference.

summary: You can now read a newborn's feeding and social cues, support bonding and responsive feeding, and act when early weight loss passes 10%. You can also say what development and growth are checked at 6 to 8 weeks and how faltering growth is defined.

A.q: A midwife is teaching new parents to recognise when their baby wants to feed. Which is an early feeding cue?
options: Crying loudly and arching
Turning the head with mouth open
Falling asleep at the breast
Turning the head away from the nipple
A.why: Rooting (turning the head and opening the mouth) is an early hunger cue; feeding at early cues is easier than waiting for crying (NHS).

whyNot.0: Crying is a late cue, by which time the baby is harder to feed.
whyNot.2: Falling asleep at the breast may be a sign of the end of a feed, not hunger.
whyNot.3: Turning away usually signals that the baby has had enough.

A.q: At the 6–8 week review, which aspects of development does NICE NG194 ask to be assessed?
options: Social smiling, visual fixing and following
Rolling over from tummy to back
Sitting with support and babbling in syllables
Reaching out and grasping toys
A.why: NG194 1.3.5: at 6 to 8 weeks, assess the baby's social smiling and visual fixing and following.

whyNot.1: Rolling over develops later in the first year and is not the NG194 6-8 week check.
whyNot.2: Sitting and babbling are later milestones, not part of the 6-8 week assessment.
whyNot.3: Reaching and grasping develop later than 6-8 weeks.

A.q: Parents ask when their breastfed baby should be back to her birth weight. According to NICE NG75, by when do most babies regain it?
options: By 5 days
By 10 days
By 6 weeks
By 3 weeks
A.why: NG75 1.1.1: weight loss usually stops after about 3-4 days, and most infants have returned to their birth weight by 3 weeks.

whyNot.0: At 5 days many babies are still below birth weight; loss has only just stopped.
whyNot.1: Many babies regain it sooner, but NG75's benchmark for most babies is 3 weeks, not 10 days.
whyNot.2: 6 weeks is later than NG75's 3-week benchmark.

B.q: Baby Sami is 5 days old and has lost 11% of his birth weight. He is breastfed and his mother says he cries before most feeds. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure, as early weight loss is normal
Advise formula top-ups after each feed
Assess him clinically and observe a feed
Reweigh him at the health visitor review
B.why: NG75 1.1.2: loss of more than 10% needs a clinical assessment for dehydration or illness, a detailed feeding history and consideration of observing a feed by a trained person.

whyNot.0: Some loss is normal, but over 10% needs assessment rather than reassurance.
whyNot.1: Routine top-ups risk ending breastfeeding; assess and support feeding first.
whyNot.3: Waiting for a later review delays assessment of a baby who has lost over 10%.

B.q: A baby has lost 12% of birth weight and a feeding plan is agreed. How often should the baby be weighed?
options: Twice a day until gaining
No more often than daily
Weekly until 6 weeks old
Before and after every feed
B.why: NG75 1.1.5: reweigh at intervals depending on the level of concern, but no more frequently than daily.

whyNot.0: Twice-daily weighing is more frequent than NICE advises.
whyNot.2: Weekly weighing is too infrequent after a loss of over 10%.
whyNot.3: Test-weighing around feeds is not recommended practice.

B.q: A breastfed baby needs a supplement after significant weight loss. Which advice follows NICE NG75?
options: Give formula first, then any breast milk
Pause breastfeeding until weight rises
Use cooled boiled water between feeds
Give any breast milk first, then formula
B.why: NG75 1.1.7: support continued breastfeeding, advise expressing, and feed any available breast milk before giving infant formula.

whyNot.0: The order is reversed: breast milk is given before formula.
whyNot.1: NICE advises supporting the mother to continue breastfeeding.
whyNot.2: Water does not provide nutrition and is not part of the plan.

C.q: At 8 weeks, a baby whose birthweight was on the 50th centile now plots on the 9th centile, having fallen across two centile spaces. How should the health professional interpret this?
options: Concern threshold met: 2 spaces
Not yet a concern until 3 spaces
Concern starts below the 0.4th
Concern starts below the 9th
C.why: NG75 1.2.1: for a birthweight between the 9th and 91st centiles, a fall across 2 or more centile spaces is a threshold for concern about faltering growth.

whyNot.1: 3 spaces is the threshold for babies whose birthweight was above the 91st centile.
whyNot.2: The 0.4th centile relates to BMI in children over 2, not weight in infants.
whyNot.3: The weight threshold regardless of birthweight is below the 2nd centile, not the 9th.

C.q: Arlo was born at 32 weeks and is now 14 weeks old. His mother asks why he has not yet smiled socially. How should his developmental age be calculated?
options: From his due date, until he is 2
From his birth date, from the start
From his due date, until 6 months
From his due date, until he is 1
C.why: For babies born prematurely, developmental age is calculated from the original due date, not the birth date, until they are 2 years old (NHS). Arlo's corrected age is about 6 weeks.

whyNot.1: Using his birth date would wrongly expect skills he is not yet due to show.
whyNot.2: Correction continues beyond 6 months, until 2 years.
whyNot.3: Correction continues beyond 1 year, until 2 years.

C.q: Chloe, 19, grew up in foster care and had an emergency caesarean. On day 3 she tells the midwife she does not yet feel close to her baby. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Recognise she may need extra bonding support
Advise her that feelings develop by themselves
Suggest formula so relatives can feed baby
Make a referral to children's social care
C.why: NG194 1.3.18-1.3.19: a traumatic birth, recovery from birth and having been through the care system can affect bonding, and these parents may need additional support, such as skin-to-skin and responding to cues.

whyNot.1: Leaving it to time misses the support NICE asks midwives to offer.
whyNot.2: Fewer people regularly feeding the baby can help bonding (NG194 1.5.19).
whyNot.3: Care experience and slow bonding are not in themselves safeguarding concerns; support comes first.

reteach.title: The baby is talking: are we listening?
reteach.question: If a newborn cannot speak, how does he tell you he is hungry, full or unwell, and what should the adults do?

blocks.body: Stirring, fist sucking and rooting say 'I am ready to feed'. Turning away and relaxed hands say 'I have had enough'. Crying says 'you missed my earlier signals'. When parents respond to cues, feeds go better and bonding grows. When a baby stops giving cues (refusing feeds, becoming less responsive), NICE asks you to treat that change seriously (NG194 1.4.7).

blocks.text: Over 10% weight loss is a trigger for assessment and feeding support, not a reason to stop breastfeeding.

explain.body: Hold the baby close, pace the feed, watch for signs the baby has had enough and do not push them to finish the bottle. Prop feeding is dangerous, and a formula-fed baby can be overfed (NG194 1.5.19).

steps.label: Watch for fullness
steps.sub: stop when baby has had enough

test.q: Which advice supports responsive bottle feeding?
options: Encourage baby to finish every bottle
Prop the bottle so baby can feed alone
Pace the feed and watch for fullness
Feed strictly every 4 hours by the clock
test.why: NG194 1.5.19: responsive bottle feeding includes pacing the feed and recognising signs that the baby has had enough milk.

whyNot.0: Pushing a baby to finish risks overfeeding.
whyNot.1: Prop feeding is dangerous and is advised against.
whyNot.3: Responsive feeding follows the baby's cues, not a fixed clock.

explain.body: NICE encourages parents to value time with their baby through face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin contact and responding appropriately to the baby's cues (NG194 1.3.17).

test.q: Which approach does NICE NG194 recommend to promote emotional attachment?
options: A fixed 4-hourly feeding schedule
Face-to-face interaction and skin-to-skin
Settling the baby to sleep in a separate room
Several relatives sharing the feeds
test.why: NG194 1.3.17: face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin contact and responding to the baby's cues promote emotional attachment.

whyNot.0: Fixed schedules do not respond to the baby's cues.
whyNot.2: Separation does not promote attachment, and safe sleep advice favours room-sharing.
whyNot.3: Minimising the number of people regularly feeding the baby can help bonding.

explain.body: Some weight loss in the first days is normal, mainly fluid. It usually stops after about 3-4 days, and most babies are back to birth weight by 3 weeks. Loss over 10% needs assessment and feeding support (NG75 1.1).

test.q: A mother asks when her baby's early weight loss will stop. What does NICE NG75 say?
options: After about 1–2 days
After about 7–10 days
After about 3–4 days
After about 14 days
test.why: NG75 1.1.1: early weight loss usually stops after about 3 or 4 days of life.

whyNot.0: 1-2 days is earlier than NG75 describes.
whyNot.1: By 7-10 days most babies are regaining weight.
whyNot.3: 14 days is too late; by then most are regaining towards birth weight.

explain.body: At 6 to 8 weeks the baby has a full examination (NIPE infant check) and NICE asks for social smiling and visual fixing and following to be assessed. Weight and head circumference are measured around 8 weeks and plotted (NG194 1.3.3, 1.3.5, 1.3.6).

head: Area
What is looked for
rows: Fixes on and follows a face

test.q: At the 6–8 week review, which finding needs further assessment?
options: Not fixing on or following a face
Weight tracking along the 50th centile
Mother reports a social smile
Head circumference on the 25th centile
test.why: Visual fixing and following is assessed at 6-8 weeks (NG194 1.3.5); its absence needs further assessment.

whyNot.1: Steady growth along a centile is reassuring.
whyNot.2: A social smile is the expected finding at this age.
whyNot.3: A head circumference on a normal centile is not a concern by itself.
